+A _generator_ represents a collection of secret files, usually generated by a script. In case the generation is not meant to be done programmatically, the files can also be imported manually via the CLI's `--set` flag (more on this later (TODO)).

+
+```nix
+{ modulesPath, ... }:
+{
+  imports = [ "${modulesPath}/security/vars.nix" ];
+}
+```
+
+Here's how a basic generator might look like:

+```nix
+{
+  vars.generators.example = {
+    backend = "plain";
+    files.example = { };
+    script =
+      pkgs:
+      pkgs.writeScript "gen-example" ''
+        #!/bin/sh
+        echo "Hewwo world!" > "$out/example"
+      '';
+  };
+}
+```
+
+For now, think of the backend field as a black box. We'll go over how backends work a bit later.
+
+One important thing to note is that we didn't directly set `script` to the path to a script. Indeed, we instead created a function from a package set to the given script. Still, the generator scripts might need to run on a different architecture than the one the NixOS system is about to be deployed to. As a result, scripts must use the package set they are given as an argument.

+Scripts (be it generator or backend scripts) can be written in any language. Throughout this document we will be mostly using Bash, although that's not a hard requirement for using vars.

+
+The CLI accepts a few different kinds of inputs. The two most important ones are `--file` and `--flake`. We'll be using the former in this document. To generate the secret described above, one can use the `generate` command:

+$ nix-cli generate -f /path/to/config

+- 'example' (file 'example' is missing)
+Evaluating prompts:
+Generating 'example'
+Successfully (re)run 1 generator(s).
+Running fixup scripts:
+- 'example' (1 files)
+```
+
+Note that this will do nothing on further re-runs! To force a generator to be re-run, one can use the `-g` flag:
+
+```
+$ nix-cli generate -f /path/to/config -g example
+Rebuild order:
+- 'example' (forced)
+Evaluating prompts:
+Generating 'example'
+Successfully (re)run 1 generator(s).
+Running fixup scripts:
+- 'example' (1 files)
+```
+
+### Generator dependencies
+
+Generators can depend on other generators. The inputs for a given generator will be available in the `$in` directory for the respective script. For example:

+```nix

+  vars.generators.derived = {
+    dependencies = [ "example" ];
+    files.derived = { };
+    script =
+      pkgs:
+      pkgs.writeScript "gen-derived" ''
+        #!/bin/sh
+        export PATH="${
+          lib.makeBinPath [
+            pkgs.coreutils
+            pkgs.cowsay
+          ]
+        }"
+        cat $in/example/example | cowsay > $out/derived
+      '';
+  };
+}
+```

+- 'derived' (file 'derived' is missing)

+Running fixup scripts:
+- 'example' (1 files)
+- 'derived' (1 files)
+```

Yes, regenerations are inherently conservative. For example, changing the generator script will not regenerate the secret either. This was an intentional design choice. Doing otherwise would require the backends to somehow keep track of the provenance of each secret (i.e. what dependencies, prompts, etc were part of its declaration). In practice, it's often useful to be able to, for example, refactor a generation script without invalidating all pre-existing keys generates by it or whatnot.

I guess the best I can do is stress this a bit harder in the documentation.

Fresh day, fresh mind. I think I have an idea of how to solve it while introducing the minimum amount of complexity (in particular, no rollbacks are necessary).

The backends would need to store additional metadata for each secret. The metadata should be treated as an opaque blob by the backends (but would contain a tiny bit of JSON). The backends would be free to encrypt the metadata, although this wouldn't be necessary for 99% of use-cases. We'd introduce a `set-meta` script (or perhaps merge this with `set`, but who knows) each backend *has* to implement. Moreover, we'd change `exists` to `get-meta` (a non existent file would return `null`). 

(hmm, now that I think about it, repurposing the `exists` command might not work, as `exists` works on a per-file basis while the metadata exists on a per-secret basis; I guess 2 new scripts is the worst case scenario).

Each secret version would have some unique ID associated with it (could be some UUID or whatever, the details don't matter). By "secret version" I mean "concrete instantiation of the secret on disk". The metadata for a file contains the IDs of every concrete dependency that went into it, together with its own ID. When running `generate`, the CLI would first topo-sort each file (as dictated by the dependency graph), then go through them one-by-one. 

A secret would get a new random ID whenever it is regenerated (or imported from an external directory with `--set`). While traversing the aforementioned topo-sorted list, we regenerate a secret if either of the following holds:
- the up-to-date list of dependencies (together with their IDs!) does not match the one saved in the metadata. This would detect added or removed edges, but would also detect new versions of the dependencies (perhaps new versions that got created in a previous run of the CLI, one that crashed!).
- `--set` or `--generate` got passed for the generator in question.

In particular, `set-meta` would only be called after everything else is done, meaning that a crash will simply make us redo the step we stopped at (and everything thereafter).

I'll try thinking about this more and bringing it up during the new meetup. Curious if you have any thoughts about the idea.

all in all looks pretty good, some discussion around fixup we still have to clarify

also the documentation should probably live somewhere in the docs tree :)

I saw many issues in this PR, many attributed to a lack of unit and integration testing. The code has not been designed with testing in mind so non interactive invocations are not possible (e.g. setting prompts automatically). 
The biggest architectural problem right now is that this is a database interface, with CRUD operations, but the backends are not receiving enough information to be able to do rollback. so right now if a generate secret fails, it will leave the secret database in a broken state.
